title: ArkBridge Dedicated Capacity Discovery
next_steps: Send Dedicated pricing and commit options by 2026-06-12
Share security and compliance deck (SOC2/ISO/KMS) link
Schedule POC scoping session with ArkBridge infra and legal - proposed week of 2026-06-22
action_items: Luis Ortega: Send Dedicated pricing spreadsheet and service level overview by 2026-06-12
Maya Chen: Prepare proposal for burst strategy (reserved + burst) and recommended VM/GPU types by 2026-06-15

summary: Discovery focused on dedicated capacity needs: reserved GPU sizing, isolation/VPC requirements, burst handling and autoscaling expectations. Customer seeks predictable latency for production scoring flows, SOC2 compliance, and options for private VPC/private deployment. Next steps: pricing, security docs, POC scoping.
transcript:
[00:00] Luis Ortega: Hey everyone thanks for joining. I’m Luis from Redwood, AE on the account. Maya our solutions engineer is here as well. How’s everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya Mehta: Doing well, thanks. We just wrapped another sprint so timing is good.
[00:10] Evan Ross: Hi all, Evan. Looking forward to understanding how dedicated works.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Great — quick agenda: high-level goals, current stack and constraints, expected traffic and latency targets, security/compliance, then we can talk about sizing and burst model. Does that sound good?
[00:22] Samir Patel: Yup, sounds good.
[00:24] Priya: Quick note — legal will probably want SOC2 docs early, just so you know.
[00:28] Luis: Totally; we’ll share that in the follow-ups.
[00:31] --- header ---
Date: 2026-06-10
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Luis Ortega (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Evan Ross (ArkBridge Head of ML), Priya Mehta (CTO), Samir Patel (Infra)
[00:45] Evan: For context we are a fintech that does near-real-time credit scoring and fraud detection. Currently we call external hosted APIs for embeddings and generation for remediation messages, but we’re hitting cost and latency issues. We want a dedicated setup to reduce unit cost and to isolate traffic — especially for PII flows.
[01:05] Maya: Got it. When you say "near-real-time" what are the latency targets and qps?
[01:10] Evan: For the scoring endpoint we need 95th < 200ms ideally, tail is important. RPS is currently modest — around 15 rps bursty peaks to ~80 rps during settlements. Token size per request varies — typical payloads 120-400 tokens, some longer debugging requests.
[01:28] Samir: And we have a compliance requirement that inference for PII stays in our VPC or on-prem. We can’t route PII to multi-tenant hosted endpoints.
[01:36] Luis: Okay that pushes towards Dedicated or Private — Dedicated gives reserved GPUs in isolated tenancy in our cloud offering, Private would be our VPC/on-prem package. Which direction are you leaning?
[01:45] Priya: We prefer Redwood Dedicated if the isolation is sufficient — we like the managed aspects and the SLA. On-prem is a heavier lift unless we need air-gap.
[01:54] Maya: Quick clarification: Dedicated provides tenant isolation at the compute level and VPC peering. We support customer-managed keys for encryption, audit logs, and SSO integrations. Private is available if you need the control plane in your network or stricter data residency.
[02:10] Evan: Good to know. About burst — we’re worried about daily settlement spikes. Can dedicated handle large bursts without overpaying for capacity we don’t use most of the time?
[02:20] Maya: Two main patterns: reserved baseline GPU pools for steady state, plus burst capacity that can be either pre-reserved smaller instances for quick warm-up or a managed burst pool that uses the provider’s on-demand capacity. We also use KV/prefix caching to keep hot contexts in memory so many calls hit cached tokens which reduces GPU work.
[02:40] Samir: How do warm-start times look? We can’t tolerate long cold starts on the scoring path.
[02:45] Maya: With dedicated pools you can keep a minimum number of replicas warm; depending on model size and quantization a warm replica is ready in seconds to low 10s of seconds. We also suggest low-latency instance types with fast NVMe to reduce startup. For the hottest flows we recommend keeping a small always-on baseline.
[03:03] Evan: Cool. What model sizes are you recommending for scoring vs NLG?
[03:07] Maya: For scoring embeddings and small classification we usually suggest a smaller dense model (like a 7B equivalent) quantized to int8/4 where possible. For NLG remediation messages you might use a 13B or 33B depending on quality needs; those will need more GPU RAM. We can map expected token costs to unit economics in the pricing doc.
[03:28] Priya: Can we pin model versions for rollouts? We want to run A/B and canary.
[03:33] Luis: Yes, Dedicated supports pinning model versions and rollout policies — canary, % rollouts, automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if latency/cost thresholds are breached.
[03:44] Evan: How about autoscaling — is it reactive or predictive? We have diurnal patterns but also these settlement spikes which are harder to predict.
[03:52] Maya: We support both. Reactive autoscaler scales on queue length and GPU utilization, with configurable cooldowns. For predictable spikes we recommend scheduled scaling (based on calendar) and a small reserved buffer for unexpected bursts. We also have an optional predictive add-on that uses historical patterns to pre-warm capacity.
[04:08] Samir: Sounds promising. Any constraints on multi-GPU models, KV cache sharing across GPUs, or sequence length limits?
[04:14] Maya: Multi-GPU sharding is supported for the larger models; KV cache is managed per request session but we can colocate sessions to GPUs to maximize cache reuse. Very long sequences will push memory; we recommend truncation or chunking and model choices tuned to your sequence length distribution.
[04:30] Priya: Security — Priya again — PCI compliance is a factor. How do you handle encryption and key management?
[04:36] Luis: We integrate with customer KMS (HSM options) for at-rest and in-transit encryption. Audit logs are exportable to your SIEM. We provide SOC2 docs and can support extra contractual controls for enterprise.
[04:47] Evan: Any PCS or data residency options in EU? We have EU customers and need to ensure data does not leave region sometimes.
[04:54] Maya: Yes, we can pin Dedicated zones to specific cloud regions and enforce regional routing. For strict residency we recommend Private (VPC or on-prem) but Dedicated in an EU region is common.
[05:05] Priya: Integration with our infra — we’re on AWS EKS and use Terraform heavily. What does the onboarding look like?
[05:12] Luis: Onboarding is usually: initial sizing workshop, provisioning of the Dedicated pool (we handle cloud infra provisioning or provide TF modules), exchange of network details for peering, and then a small POC where we run your sample workloads. We do offer Terraform modules to make infra reproducible.
[05:28] Samir: Any telemetry hooks? We need per-token cost and latency breakdowns down to route and token type.
[05:33] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, tracing, and can export traces to your observability stack.
[05:40] Evan: Cost expectations — can you ballpark cost per 1M tokens on Dedicated baseline vs hosted?
[05:46] Luis: It depends on model and utilization; as a rough example, for a 13B model on Dedicated with good utilization you might see 30-60% lower per-token cost vs hosted. We’ll send concrete pricing ranges in the spreadsheet — depends heavily on committed throughput and burst allowance.
[06:02] Priya: We’ll need the exact SLA numbers for latency and uptime. Also escalation path.
[06:07] Luis: We’ll include SLA language and contact points in the follow-up.
[06:10] Evan: On PII flows — will logs or inputs be visible to Redwood staff?
[06:14] Maya: By default logs are retained per your retention policy and access is controlled by RBAC. For Dedicated we can disable staff access to payloads and provide audit trails; for extra assurance Private lets you keep logs in your network.
[06:28] Samir: One more technical — how do you handle model updates and drift monitoring?
[06:33] Maya: We have model rollouts, A/B, and quality monitoring tied to evals and prompt sets. You can set regression alerts on a prompt set so if a model update changes outputs beyond a threshold it will alert and optionally pause rollout.
[06:45] Evan: That is useful. Ok, let’s talk timeline — we want to pilot in Q3 and have production by Q4 if feasible.
[06:53] Luis: That is reasonable; typical timeline for Dedicated POC to production is 6–12 weeks depending on compliance gates and infra approvals.
[07:00] Priya: Legal will need SOC2 and DPA. We’ll loop legal in the next thread.
[07:04] Luis: Understood. We’ll send both docs and a proposed SOW template.
[07:10] Samir: For the POC, we’ll want to run your suggested baseline with a 13B quantized for remediation messages and a 7B quantized for scoring; we’ll provide traffic replay.
[07:20] Maya: Perfect — replay works well. We’ll size the GPU pool, recommend instance types and memory.
[07:24] Evan: One operational ask — during spikes can you guarantee no noisy neighbor effects?
[07:29] Maya: Dedicated pools isolate compute — noisy neighbor is much less likely, but we also provide guardrails: per-tenant QoS, token rate limiting, and fallbacks to smaller model variants under load.
[07:41] Priya: Anything else from our side?
[07:43] Evan: Nothing else.
[07:44] Luis: Great — recap of agreed items: we’ll send pricing and SLA, security/compliance docs, proposed POC plan and scheduling options. Customer will share traffic histograms and token distributions. We’ll schedule scoping call for POC.
[07:58] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks.
[08:00] Luis: Thanks all, we’ll follow up with the materials.
[08:03] --- end ---

Notes on transcript quality: medium, some words may be transcribed imperfectly (e.g., NVMe, KV cache, names) and there are occasional overlapping comments.
